title: The Investor-Ready Story Audit
subtitle: Score whether your founder narrative is clear, credible, and specific enough to raise capital and win clients before you spend a dollar amplifying it.

questions.text: How does your pitch open with your traction?

answers.label: We are the leading or best-in-class platform for X
We have seen strong growth across our key metrics
We grew 3x last year
We went from X to Y in Z months
We went from X to Y in Z months, and I can explain the specific mechanism that drove it

questions.text: If a competitor read your homepage's first paragraph, how many sentences could they copy onto their own site without changing a word?

answers.label: Most of them. It is fairly generic by design.
At least half
Two or three sentences
One, maybe
None. Every sentence contains a number or claim only we can make.

questions.text: When you describe your market opportunity, how specific does it get?

answers.label: It is a massive market with strong tailwinds
The TAM is $X billion according to an analyst firm
The category is growing at X% annually and we are ahead of it
I can name two or three forces converging right now that did not exist 18 months ago
I can name those forces and explain why this window closes if you do not move in the next 18 months

low.headline: Your narrative is running on adjectives. That is the fastest way to lose a reader in the first 30 seconds.
low.text: Words like 'leading,' 'innovative,' and 'best-in-class' cost nothing to put in a sentence, so they prove nothing. A reader's brain files them as noise before the next sentence starts. The answer is a specific number that only you can claim. '7,000 to 700,000 users in a week' is a sentence nobody else can own. '$200M raised across clients' puts someone in a category the moment you read it. Those sentences land because they cannot be manufactured.
steps: Open your pitch deck and your homepage. Count the adjectives in the first three sentences of each.
For every adjective, ask: what specific number could replace this? If you cannot find one, the claim probably is not real yet.
Pick the one number you are most proud of and rebuild your opening around it. One specific sentence beats five superlatives.

mid.headline: You have real numbers but you are not putting them at the front of the story.
mid.text: You know your traction. The problem is you are leading with context and saving the proof for later. By the time you get to the number, the reader has already formed an impression, and vague openings tend to form vague impressions.
steps: Identify the single most specific number you own. Not a range. Not a projection. The actual number.
Put it in the first sentence of your pitch, your homepage, and your LinkedIn headline. See what it does to the conversation.
Add the mechanism: not just 'we went from X to Y' but the specific thing that made it happen. The number gets attention. The mechanism earns credibility.

high.headline: You lead with specifics. The next layer is making the mechanism behind them impossible to ignore.
high.text: Specificity gets you in the room. The mechanism, the 'here is exactly why it happened and why it is repeatable,' is what keeps you there. Most founders stop at the number. The ones who close explain what is underneath it.
steps: For each core number in your narrative, write one sentence explaining why a competitor could not replicate it in the same timeframe.
Test your category timing argument: can you name three specific forces that make this inevitable right now? If you cannot say it in 90 seconds, it is not tight enough.
Ask someone outside your industry to read your homepage cold. If they cannot tell you the one number that makes you different, the specificity is not landing yet.

questions.text: When you look at your last ten pieces of content or outreach, what number are you most focused on?

answers.label: Total impressions, reach, or follower growth
Engagement rate, likes, or comments
Profile visits or link clicks
Replies or conversations started
Discovery calls booked or warm introductions made to investors or clients

questions.text: A post got 300 impressions and booked two investor conversations. Another got 40,000 impressions and booked none. Which one shapes what you publish next?

answers.label: The 40,000-impression post. Visibility compounds over time.
Probably the 40,000 one, though I suspect that is the wrong call
I would want to understand why each performed the way it did before deciding
The 300-impression post, though I would still feel pressure about the low numbers
The 300-impression post, no hesitation. I know which scoreboard matters.

questions.text: How do you currently measure whether your content or outreach is actually working?

answers.label: I do not have a real system. I publish and see what happens.
I watch likes, comments, and shares
I track clicks to my site or profile views
I log replies and the quality of inbound conversations
I can trace specific deals, intros, and meetings directly back to pieces of content

low.headline: You are running your strategy off a dashboard that cannot tell you if you are winning.
low.text: Attention feels like progress because it is visible and immediate. Revenue attribution is slower and harder to see, so it loses the argument every time someone pulls up a dashboard. I mapped these two scoreboards side by side and they almost never come from the same posts. The founders who raise and close enterprise clients are almost never the ones with the best engagement rates.
steps: Pull your last ten posts. Next to each one, write how many conversations it started and how many of those went anywhere. That is your real scorecard.
For the next 30 days, track one number only: meetings booked from content or outreach. See how that changes what you decide to publish.
Find the lowest-impression piece you published in the last quarter and check whether it actually drove any conversations you remember. You might be surprised.

mid.headline: You know which scoreboard matters. You are still letting the wrong one influence your decisions.
mid.text: Knowing that impressions are not the goal and actually running your strategy off something else are two different things. The pull toward vanity metrics is real because they are immediate. The metrics that matter usually show up weeks later, which is exactly why they keep losing the argument.
steps: Before you decide whether to publish something, ask: who specifically would this put me in front of? Not how many people might see it.
Keep a simple log: date published, impressions, conversations started, outcome. Review it monthly. Patterns become obvious faster than you expect.
Identify the one post in your history that drove the most real business. Ask what made it different from the posts that got more impressions.

high.headline: You are measuring what matters. The gap is usually in volume and consistency, not strategy.
high.text: Once you are tracking meetings and pipeline over impressions, the question shifts from 'what should I post' to 'how do I do more of what works.' That is a much better problem to have.
steps: Document the format and angle of your highest-converting posts. You probably have a pattern. If you can name it, you can repeat it.
The next time a piece gets high impressions and no calls, treat it as useful data. What is missing is probably the specific credibility signal that makes someone want to reach out.
Check whether your call to action is specific enough. Something that puts a real next step in front of the right person, not just an invitation to follow.

questions.text: If an investor asks 'why is your category inevitable right now?' how do you answer?

answers.label: It is a huge market and the technology is finally catching up
We are seeing strong tailwinds and customer adoption is accelerating
I can point to two or three recent signals: regulatory shifts, customer behavior changes, or competitive moves
I can name three forces converging right now that did not exist 18 months ago and explain why each one matters
I can do that and explain why a founder who raised in this category two years ago has a structurally different story than mine today

questions.text: How does your narrative account for the current funding environment, where AI absorbed roughly 80% of Q1 2026 venture capital?

answers.label: It does not yet. I am still working on getting the core narrative right.
I mention AI briefly but mostly focus on differentiation from direct competitors
I can clearly explain our relationship to AI, whether central or adjacent, and why that positioning matters
I can explain that relationship and give specific reasons why it strengthens my category case with this particular investor class
I know which investors are writing checks in my category right now and I have built the narrative around what they need to hear

questions.text: How does your story explain why you, specifically, are the right person to build this at this moment?

answers.label: I have the domain expertise and the team. That is the argument.
I have been in this space for X years and I understand the customer deeply
I have a specific insight or unfair advantage I can point to, not just tenure
I can connect my background to a specific capability that matters in this category right now at this stage
The reason I am right for this builds directly into the reason the category is inevitable. They are the same story.

low.headline: You can describe your business. You have not yet made the case that this category is inevitable right now.
low.text: Growing 3x does not close rounds on its own anymore. Every founder in a live deal has a growth number. The ones getting checks can articulate why their category is inevitable right now, in addition to showing that their business is working. Those are two different arguments and you need both.
steps: Write down three things that changed in your category in the last 18 months. Not 'AI is everywhere.' Specific changes, with dates if you can find them.
For each one, finish this sentence in writing: 'This matters for my company specifically because...' If you cannot finish it cleanly, the force is not specific enough.
Ask yourself what a founder raising in this category two years ago would have said. How is your answer different? That delta is your timing argument.

mid.headline: You have a timing argument. It is not yet tight enough to land in the first two minutes.
mid.text: Investors writing non-AI checks in 2026 have seen enough pivot decks to spot a thin connection fast. If your category case requires more than 90 seconds to set up, you will lose the room before you get to the good part.
steps: Practice your 'why inevitable right now' answer in exactly 60 seconds. Record it. Listen back. If it sounds like a hedge, it is.
Find one investor or advisor outside your category and pitch the timing argument cold. If they cannot repeat back the core insight in their own words, it is not clear enough.
Tighten the 'why you, why now' connection. The strongest version is when your founder story and your category timing argument are the same sentence, not two separate sections of the pitch.

high.headline: Your category case is solid. The next level is making it impossible to separate you from this moment.
high.text: The founders I watch get funded in this environment almost always share one thing: you cannot hear their pitch without understanding why they, specifically, at this specific moment, are the right bet. That is a narrative argument, not a credential one.
steps: Test whether your timing argument survives a 'so what' challenge from a skeptical investor. What happens if they say they heard this story from five other founders this month?
Make sure your category inevitability argument appears in the first two sentences of your pitch, not as a conclusion at the end.
Consider whether you are making this argument publicly, not just in pitch meetings. If the category is inevitable and you know it, are you saying so in front of the audience that needs to hear it?

questions.text: Before your last significant investor or enterprise client pitch, how many people in the process already knew your name?

answers.label: Almost none. I was starting cold across the board.
One or two out of every ten contacts had some familiarity
Roughly a third had seen something from me or heard my name
More than half had a touchpoint with my work before I sent the first message
Most were warm before contact. I barely sent a cold outreach in the whole process.

questions.text: How would you describe your current inbound from investors or enterprise clients?

answers.label: I do not have inbound. Everything comes from outbound.
Occasional inbound, usually low quality or not the right fit
Some inbound, but I am not sure what is driving it
Regular inbound I can trace to specific posts, talks, or publications
Most of the deals I care about are warm before I reach out. People contact me having already decided I am worth talking to.

questions.text: When you are about to reach out to an investor or a potential enterprise client cold, what is your actual starting point?

answers.label: I write the message, personalize it a bit, and send it
I research them first and try to find a relevant angle
I have usually engaged with their content or found a mutual connection before reaching out
I usually have a reason they have already seen something from me: a post, a talk, a mutual intro
By the time I reach out, I am rarely starting cold. I have been building toward that conversation for months.

low.headline: You are doing everything right except the part that happens before the pitch.
low.text: The founders I watch get funded in this environment almost always share one thing: the room already knows them before the cold email arrives. That warm room is harder to build than any stat in a deck, but it is also more durable than any single pitch.
steps: Map out the 20 investors or clients who matter most to your next 90 days. Before you send anything, ask honestly: does this person know my name? Have they seen my work?
Start publishing around the specific insight that makes your category inevitable. Not company updates. The actual point of view behind why you are right.
Identify one event, publication, or platform where your target investors or clients are paying attention. Show up there with a real point of view before you need anything from them.

mid.headline: You have some warmth in the room. It is not systematic yet.
mid.text: Knowing that warm outreach converts better is one thing. Having built the audience that makes it possible is a different problem entirely, and it almost always gets solved under time pressure if it gets solved at all.
steps: Audit your inbound from the last six months. Where did it come from: which posts, talks, or introductions? Do more of that, less of everything else.
Find one investor or enterprise client who came inbound and ask them exactly what made them reach out. Their answer is the most valuable data you have about your story.
Build a 90-day warm-room plan before your next raise or enterprise push. Not a content calendar. A specific list of people you want to be warm to you, and a concrete plan for getting there.

high.headline: You have built the warm room. Make sure the story preceding you is the right one.
high.text: When people know you before you reach out, the narrative you have put into the world becomes the frame for every conversation. That is a real advantage. It also means the quality of what you are saying publicly matters more than the volume of it.
steps: Audit what someone learns about you from the first three things they find when they search your name. Is that story coherent with what you are about to pitch them?
The risk at this stage is that your public narrative is built around an older version of your company or thesis. Make sure the warm room you have built matches the story you are telling in the room.
Check whether your warm-room advantage is concentrated in one channel or platform. Single-channel dependence is a real risk. Company page reach has dropped roughly 60% since 2024.

questions.text: Who publishes most of the content that represents your company to investors and potential clients?

answers.label: Mainly the brand page or our marketing team
Roughly split between the company page and my personal profile
Mostly my personal profile, but I still invest real time in the brand page
Primarily me in the first person. The brand page handles company news.
Me personally, with a real point of view and my face on it. The brand page is secondary and I know it.

questions.text: The last time you published something under your own name, how personal was it?

answers.label: It was a product update or a company announcement
It was a thought piece but written in a polished, brand-appropriate voice
It had a real opinion but was still fairly safe and professional
It shared a specific lesson from a hard week, a mistake I made, or a number I actually own
It was something I almost did not publish because it felt too specific or too honest, and it outperformed everything else

questions.text: When someone reads your LinkedIn headline or founder bio cold, what do they walk away knowing?

answers.label: My title and company name
My title, company name, and the category we are in
What we do and roughly who we do it for
What we do, who we do it for, and a specific number that puts us in a category
Exactly what I have built, why it matters right now, and why I am credible to build it, in one reading

low.headline: You are hiding behind the brand when the brand needs you in front of it.
low.text: I have watched seed-stage founders consistently outperform their own company pages with worse design and no ad budget, just because the post came from a person instead of a logo. LinkedIn company page reach has dropped roughly 60% since 2024. The brand page matters for some things. You are the distribution. The brand page is what you send people to after they already trust you.
steps: For the next 30 days, publish nothing on the company page that you have not first published under your own name. See what the numbers look like.
Write one post this week in plain language about something at the company that did not go the way you wanted. Not a crisis communication. A real observation from someone building.
Ask yourself: if someone discovers my company through my profile, do they find a founder they would want to talk to, or a logo they can Google?

mid.headline: You are posting as a founder. The content still reads like a brand.
mid.text: Putting your name on a post is not the same as putting a point of view in it. The posts that drive conversations for founders tend to be specific, plainly written, and a little uncomfortable to publish.
steps: Look at your last five posts and count how many you could have published without your specific company context. If the answer is more than two, the posts are not specific enough to you.
Find one thing you know about your category that most people in it get wrong. Write a post about the insight itself, not your product. See what it does.
Read back the last post you published. Would a stranger know from reading it that you are someone worth having a conversation with?

high.headline: You are the face of the story. Make sure the story you are telling is the right one.
high.text: When you are the distribution, the quality of your narrative matters more than the volume of your publishing. You have solved the distribution problem. The work now is making sure what comes through it is specific, credible, and puts the right people in conversation with you.
steps: Audit the last ten posts for specificity: how many contained a number, a direct quote, or a lesson tied to a specific event? Those are the posts that build the warm room.
Make sure your LinkedIn headline and bio are doing the same work as your best posts. If your headline still reads like a job title, it is undercutting the rest of your content.
Check whether the posts that got the most impressions were also the ones that started the most conversations. If not, you have probably already figured out which direction to move in.

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: In 30 minutes I'll show you which two gaps to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing.

persona_selector.text: Where are you in the fundraising cycle right now?

answers.label: Pre-seed (building the story before the first raise)
Seed-stage (actively pitching or preparing to)
Post-Series A (raising growth capital and closing enterprise clients)
Growth stage (the narrative is the bottleneck to the next round)
